reason: This passage (Genesis 34) is heavily populated with regular human characters who speak, express emotions, and voice opinions. The characters include Dinah, Shechem, Hamor, Jacob, Simeon, Levi, and the men of the city. Shechem expresses love ('his soul cleaved to Dinah'; וַתִּדְבַּק נַפְשׁוֹ בְּדִינָה) and desire for the young woman. Jacob's sons express anger (וַיִּחַר לָהֶם מְאֹד) and grief (וַיִּתְעַצְּבוּ) at the violation. Throughout the narrative, multiple characters engage in direct dialogue—Shechem negotiates with his father, Hamor negotiates with Jacob's family, Jacob's sons present their condition regarding circumcision, and the city men deliberate on intermarriage. Jacob expresses his concerns and complaints to Simeon and Levi about their violent retaliation. Simeon and Levi voice their indignation with a rhetorical response. The passage is fundamentally character-driven narrative featuring ordinary humans (not divine beings) with clearly articulated emotions, opinions, and motivations.
